title: Shortest paths from one source with Dijkstra
prompt: Implement networkDelayTime(times [][]int, n int, k int) int. Nodes are labelled 1..n and times holds directed edges {u, v, w} with a positive travel time w. A signal starts at node k. Return how long it takes to reach every node, or -1 if some node is unreachable.
explanation: This is Dijkstra: keep a tentative distance per node, repeatedly settle the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance, and relax its outgoing edges. Settling in increasing-distance order is what makes a settled node final, so you never revisit one. The answer is the largest settled distance, and an unsettled node at the end means unreachable. The scan for the minimum is O(n) here, which is fine for a dense graph; swap it for a heap when the graph is sparse.
hints: Start every node at a value larger than any real total, and the source at zero.
Each round, pick the cheapest node you have not finished with yet, then improve its neighbours through it.
Parallel edges and edges back to the source are normal input, so only ever lower a distance, never overwrite it.

title: Substring search without rewinding
prompt: Implement strStr(haystack, needle string) int returning the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack, or -1. An empty needle is 0. It must run in O(len(haystack)+len(needle)): the tests include a 200k haystack of one repeated letter that a restart-on-mismatch scan will not finish.
explanation: KMP. First build the prefix table lps, where lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of needle[:i+1] that is also a suffix of it. Then walk the haystack with a match length k and, on a mismatch, fall back to lps[k-1] instead of restarting: the fallback is exactly how much of the needle you have already confirmed. The haystack index never moves backwards, so the scan is linear. The table is built by running the same fallback loop of the needle against itself.
hints: After a mismatch you already know the last few characters you consumed. How much of the pattern do they still satisfy?
Build the table with the same loop you use for the search, matching the pattern against itself starting one position in.
The outer index over the text should only ever increase; only the match length may drop.
refs: LC 28 Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String

title: A Fenwick tree for mutable range sums
prompt: Implement a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree over ints. NewFenwick(nums []int) *Fenwick builds it, Add(i, delta int) adds delta to index i, and Sum(l, r int) int returns the inclusive sum of indices l..r. Both Add and Sum must be O(log n): the tests do 100k updates and 100k queries.
explanation: Index j of the tree stores the sum of the j & (-j) elements ending at j, using 1-based internal indices so that the low bit is meaningful. An update walks upward with j += j & (-j), touching every node whose range covers the position; a prefix query walks downward with j -= j & (-j), stripping one low bit at a time and adding each block it lands on. Both loops run once per set bit, so both are O(log n). A range sum is two prefix sums subtracted.
hints: Keep the array one longer than the input and treat position i as internal index i+1; internal index 0 has no low bit to strip and would loop forever.
The isolated lowest set bit of j is j & (-j). One direction adds it, the other subtracts it: adding climbs to the parent that also covers you, subtracting jumps to the block before yours.
Build by calling your update once per element rather than writing a separate construction rule.
refs: LC 315 Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
